items.body: From noise to nice. Harsh to honed. Squelch to sculpture. Ectospasm is a 10/10 top-tier proposition for anyone still prepared to leave the comfort of the known and go poking around in whatever is moving about underneath it. Stomping through a distorting ping and brace-breakbeat Ectospasm by Myoptik   Now that’s more like it. Production pushed deeper into the exploratory, the exploratory pushed deeper into the production, atmospheres absolutely everywhere on Myoptik‘s latest drop Ectospasm. Eight experimental sculptures, two of which are, for reasons that remain gloriously inexplicable, fifteen-minute attention-stretching time-space continuum-ripping mind-warping rational-pondering joy events, taking us somewhere between possibility and potential while making a quite deliberate decision not to run with the pack. Which is probably why, by the time we emerge, we are unequivocally not the same creation that pressed the first triangle and set track one loose. There is parasitic dalliance via opener “Framez v4.” Breaks. Squelches. Drum with bass, drum without bass, things behaving like drum and bass while being absolutely, defiantly, not drum and bass. That’s not drum and bass. Later, malfunctioning ambience a​rrives with the express intention of making relaxation impossible. Big fat industriana follows, metal-bashing its way through both form and formlessness, while the machinery seems increasingly uncertain about whether it is machinery at all. Then comes the epic whale of time that is “Dirt stoP Pt2″—and yes, that very awkward capital P is a tell—stomping through a distorting ping and brace-breakbeat, vocal treatments twitching at the edges while bubbling synths disappear down some kind of mycelium reverie. It’s enormous. It’s odd. It takes its time. It does not apologise for any of this. The first of our fifteen-minute treats is the caterwauling, mind-expanding throwdown of “Dungeon Stalker E,” a thing that thrashes your backside onto the floor and then protests at every subsequent attempt to stay still. And this, folks of all genders, is where those with enough gall—or precisely the right concoction of consciousness—to keep up for its full duration may well have attained legendary status. Absolutely wicked belter of a tune. The kind that turns up halfway through a collection and suddenly puts the whole damn thing in my top ten of the year. Spanking, dog-down-deep, dirty shizzle. A proper monster. Completely bent-out-of-shape genre-hybridizing :: And somewhere across all this glorious disobedience is perhaps the most diverse, inclusive and completely bent-out-of-shape genre-hybridizing archetype for modern times you’re likely to encounter. Ectospasm doesn’t just blur the boundaries between genres; it seems to regard the boundaries themselves as an outdated administrative error. Everything gets invited. Everything gets mangled. Everything gets a turn. Breakbeat, noise, ambience, industrial, squelch, electronics and whatever else happens to wander into the room are thrown into the same beautifully dysfunctional ecosystem and left to figure out their own relationships. And that’s really the thing with Ectospasm. It routinely refuses to play the game. It doesn’t seem particularly interested in familiarity, conformity, genre obedience or that increasingly tedious practice of self-aggrandising pastiche where the safest way to sound new is apparently to sound exactly like the people you already know. This is not lazy music. It is music working. Properly working. Working at the listener. Working on the listener. Working hard enough to create the possibility of something happening that wasn’t already there when you pressed play. And because of that, it is absolutely full of potential. From noise to nice. Harsh to honed. Squelch to sculpture. Ectospasm is a 10/10 top-tier proposition for anyone still prepared to leave the comfort of the known and go poking around in whatever is moving about underneath it. Opening with a barrage of video-game clicks and cuts, delicately woven blips give way on “Pxlrn” to explosive breakbeat strata, while “Tlrnc.0” and “Plk3rn” maneuver through mechanically shaved and articulated rhythms. Less a collection of disheveled pieces than a study in disjointed layers connecting, the record gradually reveals complex and creative broken-electro-nic forms. Highlights “Trsh_Lp” and “Glnch.v2” take shape through morphing, Autechre, Alva Noto, and Suumhow-shaped crevasses, as Potato.exe generates several miles of crunched, sound-scraping beats on this inaugural ERR_SESSION series. “Vctr_∅∅” dives deeper into rugged terrain, opening up experimental avenues without losing its focus. This downtempo foray into glitch and grit closes with the head-bobbing final chapter, “Klmn0,” bringing everything together in one fell swoop of cohesive flutter. items.body: Rather than simply calling out for someone to remain, Geyzel uses these five tracks to explore what happens when you finally stop holding everything in. Its hidden strength is found in that openness: a willingness to wander through uncertainty, sit with absence, and ultimately let it all out. Stay. opens into a more vulnerable space Five tracks make up Serge Geyzel’s Stay. EP, revealing a different side of the multi-talented Saratov, Russia and Berlin, Germany-based sound sculptor. While analog gear and synthesizer production remain firmly at its core, this release opens into a more vulnerable space, where emotion slowly rises through ambient passages and drifting acoustic waves, as heard on the opening title track. Geyzel’s sleek electronic instincts are still present, but Stay. takes a looser, more exploratory route, moving through downtrodden jazz, hip-hop breaks, and fractured rhythms. “Some of It I Am Not” seems to unravel in fragments, gathering scattered thoughts and feelings along the way. As the EP unfolds, “But Then I Met You (for SF)” carries that wandering, Teebs-like sensibility into more uncertain territory, its searching quality sounding almost like a message sent toward someone, something, or perhaps life and love itself. Closer “Let’s Continue from the Beginning” feels like a long-lost sibling to that sentiment, bringing the journey full circle without quite resolving it. The penultimate “Pseudonostalgia” is perhaps the EP’s quietest revelation. Cruising under the radar, it evokes the strange sensation of remembering ​an event you never actually experienced—something unfolding somewhere deep in the background, half-formed and difficult to place. Acoustic instruments, samples, and distant voices gradually shed layers of melancholy, giving the piece a ghostly sense of memory. The liner notes describe the emotional distortion of time that comes with missing someone, particularly when longing for their return. That feeling sits at the heart of Stay. Rather than simply calling out for someone to remain, Geyzel uses these five tracks to explore what happens when you finally stop holding everything in. Its hidden strength is found in that openness: a willingness to wander through uncertainty, sit with absence, and ultimately let it all out. Stay. is available on Bandcamp. items.body: Luca Young crafts a hypnagogic birthing enclosure in the space created by this music, a space open for manifesting further gifts of reflective imagination. A sun shower appears, a brief trickle of luminescent moments Infinite Lovers, Pt. I by Luca Young   Electric guitar glitch swims in out of phase and out of focus photographs recovered from a forgotten SD card on the first song, “Welcome to the Other Side.” It reminds me of the skipping CDs used by the likes of Oval, clicks stuttering over top of field recordings of what sound like an airport or train station (a place of departure and return). It’s arrival music from the place we’ve departed from. These mesmeric textured loops are structured around they hypnotic guitar lines, themselves looping. All cascade and oscillate into the fog of timbral static coming off the Pacific. A disconsolate chord bathed in tape hiss and pitch shifted down starts “Pygmy Song.” The listening mind is teased by moments of reversed loops and the slide of fingers across the strings while glassy electronics appear for brief seconds in moments of fragility. Voices in staccato are cut and chopped alongside noisy high pitched tones who never overstay their welcome. It’s the music of dream memory trying to be captured and held onto, slipping away before it is fully grasped. On “7073” pensive upbeat strings meet with bo​uncing ball sounds and echo effects before swimming into crystalline pools of translucent electro refraction. Sounds of wave release the surf to the shore, and liquid textures. Small schools of musical fish swarm together for a moment, then separate in the drift of gentle abstract pulses and beats, the glitter of tiny notes surfacing for a second and then disappearing back into the deep. A sun shower appears, a brief trickle of luminescent moments. Directing the awakening of energy at the base of the spine :: The sound of planes rising or descending and further airport like sounds merge in a miasmic gloop at the beginning of “Kundalini.” The woman’s voice over the loudspeaker is comforting, directing the awakening of energy at the base of the spine, third eye subtly tingling by the luminescent vibrations. Further voices seem to be run through a gated sequencer, garbled through formant filters, language reduced to phonemes in a downtempo melodic style then disappears along the drift of a smoothly changing line. Infinity is in the distance. Part I of Infinite Lovers ends with the fifth track, “Ethiopia.” It’s starts with the ripple of tinkling pianos before building up successive pressure with louder playing, swoops of textural noise, warbling sonic transformations, glitch patterns, and long sweeps of filled with emotional grain. On this release Luca Young “was stepping into new territory artistically, moving away from a previous project. I decided to release this music under my given name, shedding an old artistic identity. It felt like the right move — a more honest expression of the kind of music I wanted to make.” The music is honest and unpretentious, warm and inviting. Leaving the skin of the old projects behind, he takes the listener on a voyage to the other side. It will be exciting to hear what comes with Part II. Infinite Lovers, Pt. I is available on Lōʻihi. items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The serial production aimed to expose the artifice behind the image, a concept applicable to any work conveying an underlying message. In this instance, it is music... which, through repetition, reveals itself to be more than it initially appeared. The cover of Taking Tiger Mountain (By Strategy) offers a clue as to what is going on. Several things happen simultaneously. Eno's calm vocals on "Burning Airlines Give You So Much More" head in one direction, while the guitars perform a different function; they are superimposed layers, much like Andy Warhol's serial-style photographs. The repetitive modal texture is merely the starting point for this game of Chinese boxes, which, when opened, reveal something different, something new. Something about "Back In Judy's Jungle" reminds me of those strange pop songs by 60s psychedelic bands, tracks with a circus-like atmosphere, such as Pink Floyd's "See Emily Play.""The Fat Lady of Limbourg" is more futuristic, closer to Krautrock and quintessentially Eno, featuring the songwriting style and vocal approach that remain constant regardless of the musical vehicle. After all, there is the playful, simpler Eno, or rather, a simplicity that emerges from complexity, and the openly experimental Eno, with echoes of Roxy Music in the mix. The track features electronic effects and Andy Mackay on saxophone, sounding like the wind-instrument simulators Eno would use later in his career (on Nerve Net, 1992), which once again interrupt and fracture the tempo. Nothing here is quite what it seems.Mother Whale Eyeless features Phil Collins on drums, a longtime friend of Eno who, at the time, was eager to collaborate on any experimental project that came along. Their experimental sensibilities meshed well, allowing them to find the spaces to transform the drums into yet another melodic instrument; they introduced variations that added color and diverse pitch ranges to the track, complementing the work done on guitar, given Phil Manzanera's presence throughout the album. Polly Eltes' guest vocals enhance those aforementioned higher registers... especially since the bass line later brings the pitch back down.The Great Pretender returns with dark Krautrock; we give thanks for the 1975 setting and the era of Eno's "albums", records that did more than just scratch the surface or float aimlessly, instead digging deep to reach new horizons, even when those horizons lay in unexpected places. Robert Wyatt handles percussion and Phil Manzanera plays differently, distorted, just as Eno sings differently: in a deep voice, enunciating deliberately, and slowing down his guitar, which seems to ooze as if made of fuel."Third Uncle" seems to begin with Roger Waters' bass, but Brian Turrington (who had previously played with Manzanera on Diamond Head) quickly launches into a tour de force, a race against time, while the Roxy Music guitarist does what he does best: transporting us from the known world to another dimension or universe, without spaceships or artificial substances, relying solely on the power of the mind and the act of listening. The composition was, of course, Eno's work; he adds weight to the notes and accelerates his vocal delivery, bordering on rapping, while the bass and guitar keep pace with his rapid-fire style, creating a true sonic experience. He would later elicit a similar approach from The Edge on U2's Zooropa, an album Eno was also involved in.The Portsmouth Sinfonia handles the strings on "Put A Straw Under Baby", a sound that is somewhat symphonic and childlike, yet also evokes a dockside atmosphere, with a deliberately nomadic feel. Vocal groups play a pivotal role on "Taking Tiger Mountain"; Randi & The Pyramids join Eno on "The True Wheel," creating a strange, postmodern pop-soul sound that even veers into punk and, thanks to Manzanera, experimental territory."China My China," once again featuring Robert Wyatt, sets out to subvert standard time signatures, incorporating atonal guitar work and the sounds of typewriters, alongside funky guitar lines.The title track closes the album; it is almost an elegy, one of those melancholic odes that are quintessentially Eno. Indeed, this is an album containing many Enos, and each distinct version faithfully represents the original. Yet there is no single original; there are many. There is the Krautrock Eno, the Fusion Eno, the Psychedelic, the Electronic, the Art-focused, and the Simple Eno, the latter being the persona he always chooses for his farewells, promising to return with a soul chorus that touches the very soul.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There is a piggy bank here, and inside it lie precious treasures, such as the debut of one of the great voices: that of Francesco Di Giacomo.The first of the coins stored within is the track titled "R.I.P." (Requiescant In Pace); here, Renato D'Angelo (bass) and Marcello Todaro (guitar) adopt a jazz-infused style, playing with a rhythm and speed that transcend the composition itself, revealing their sheer eagerness to play. While Gianni Nocenzi plays the piano, his brother Vittorio Nocenzi delivers a solo that straddles the line between psychedelia and the Canterbury scene. This very special piggy bank holds coins with two sides, and even three (thanks to that third dimension). That is why the piano takes on a classical tone, mirroring the vocals of Francesco Di Giacomo, a voice destined to be unforgettable from the very first moment you hear it.Passaggio features a harpsichord played by Vittorio Nocenzi; how could one not be captivated by this second "coin", small, yet equally valuable and memorable?Metamorfosi is that elusive coin, kept despite being worn and of dubious origin, whose relief is bold enough to carve out a place in the collection through the sheer force of its hammering piano, like a suite for tails and piano... yet it then mutates, hence the name, into an underground adventure where guitar and organ forge a path through subway tunnels. It is astonishing when the organ takes over the bass lines and the instruments swap roles, all held together by Pier Luigi Calderoni, who constantly shifts rhythms on the drums. When Marcello Todaro enters, he plays with wild, piercing intensity on the electric guitar, while the piano continues with classical scales. This is what should be shown to anyone wanting to experience progressive rock at its peak, music that was once new, wild, and unexpected, and which remains so to this day.Il Giardino Del Mago is the fourth coin... its origin is undetermined, no one knows how it got there, yet it is the oldest and most valuable. It is carved into four parts, with its faces divided. After some choral passages, a hard-rock sound erupts, accompanied by organ, reminiscent of early Deep Purple in its wildness, were it not for the heavily dramatic, operatic, and Mediterranean elements.The second side picks up the pace; the organ, piano, and guitar are just as important as Francesco's tenor voice. In "Chi Ride E Chi Geme," the Emerson, Lake & Palmer-style rush pauses to give way to a section reminiscent of Pink Floyd, evoking Obscured by Clouds, though only until the piano shifts into a classical mode... and everyone joins in singing. Marcello Todaro also features on the third side, with Gianni Nocenzi playing the clarinet as an ancient, distinctly Italian melody blends with progressive rock."Compenetrazione" represents the final side of the coin, where an acoustic guitar heralds the beginning of the end. Such a refined composition is hardly surprising for a 1972 debut, it is a track held in especially high regard. "Traccia" serves as the classical coda they would revisit from time to time, almost a private anthem the group kept for themselves. It is sung by the sextet in a spirit of communion akin to a secret society, a ritualistic bond that seemed to guarantee artistic success.

items.body: Review by OlyaBeginner — Listening to 'Never for Ever' felt like entering a strange emotional and almost theatrical world. I am not an expert in Kate Bush's music, so I approached the album mostly through my own feelings, images, and associations. What impressed me most is how freely she plays with her voice which becomes almost another instrument.1. BabooshkaA very playful and energetic song with a bright sound that immediately sparks emotions. There is something almost mischievous about it. At first, the music feels light and catchy, but underneath it there is a rather bitter and complicated story about love, jealousy, and mistrust. I really like this contrast between the almost cheerful sound and the darker emotions behind it.2. DeliusThis song is very strange and mysterious, but in a beautiful way. It creates an almost magical atmosphere, as if the listener is entering another world. The sound feels peaceful but also slightly unreal. It elevates the soul to another level and leaves me with the feeling of being somewhere far away from ordinary life.3. Blow AwayMy favourite song on the album. There is such an interesting play with Kate Bush's voice here. She seems to move between different emotional states, and the song feels almost theatrical. It charges me with energy while making me feel something tragic and elevated at the same time. There is a strange combination of excitement and sadness that I find incredibly beautiful.4. All We Ever Look ForA very strong song with a lot of emotional power. It feels as if it can touch something deep inside the listener. To be honest, I did not understand the meaning of it at first. After thinking about it more, I see it as a song about family, inheritance, and the things people spend their lives searching for. We inherit things from our parents, leave the family home, and then continue searching for love, security, meaning, or something that will finally make us feel complete.I especially like the musical instruments and the sound design. The song feels almost restless, as if the music itself is constantly searching for something that it cannot quite find.5. EgyptThis one feels mysterious and theatrical. It has a strong progressive-rock feeling to me, although it also sounds experimental and almost cinematic. The music creates the impression of travelling through a strange landscape. I like how different this song feels from the more intimate pieces on the album.6. The Wedding ListSuch a great song. I love the dramatic progression and the way the story unfolds. Kate Bush almost seems to be telling a fairy tale before sleep, but it is a very dark fairy tale. The music gradually becomes more intense, and the story feels increasingly dramatic. I really enjoy how she combines storytelling, theatrical performance, and music.7. ViolinSuper rock'n'roll and incredibly energetic. This song feels wild and almost uncontrollable. It has a completely different energy from the quieter and more mysterious songs on the album. I especially like the feeling of movement and excitement it creates.8. The Infant KissSuper creepy.The song is deeply unsettling. What makes it even more disturbing is the contrast between the beautiful, almost delicate sound and the uncomfortable subject matter. It creates a feeling that something is not quite right, even when the music itself sounds beautiful.9. Night Scented StockExtremely beautiful. This song creates such a delicate and almost dreamlike atmosphere. It feels as if the music is floating rather than moving forward. Once again, Kate Bush's voice contributes enormously to this feeling. It elevates my soul and creates a sense of peace and mystery.10. Army DreamersI love this song. It is heartbreaking and sad, but there is also something very beautiful and restrained about it. The sound feels almost permeated by sadness.The song is about a mother grieving for her son who has died as a soldier. But listening to it today, I could not help thinking about my own generation. Many young people were raised with the idea that the world was moving toward peace, cooperation, and friendship between countries. Hearing a song about a young life being destroyed by war therefore feels painfully relevant today.What makes the song especially powerful is that it does not sound aggressive. It sounds almost gentle, which makes the tragedy even stronger.11. BreathingThis is probably the song that shocked me the most.The song is written from the perspective of a fetus that is still inside the womb but is already aware of the terrifying world outside. The fetus is frightened by nuclear destruction and wonders what kind of world it is going to be born into.The line about dying "without" breathing is especially powerful because the word remains incomplete until the very end. Only then do we understand what is missing: breathing itself. The song connects the most basic condition of life with the possibility of nuclear destruction.And this is what makes the song so frighteningly relevant. It was written decades ago, but the fear behind it has not disappeared. It is deeply disturbing that humanity is still capable of threatening itself with weapons that could destroy the world. The song makes me think about how reckless it is to treat such a possibility as a political instrument.So, Never for Ever feels to me like an album about things that are difficult to explain directly: love, fear, family, death, war, desire, memory, and the strange feeling of being alive. What I admire most is her ability to transform emotions into characters, voices, and almost theatrical scenes, so the listener can experience the world she is creating.

items.body: Review by anomalocaris — This is an album I really love.Cressida's second album 'Asylum' differs quite a lot from their debut album. I will admit that I haven't listened to the entirety of their first album, but from the few songs I've heard, it sounds like some pretty decent rock. Asylum brings a new symphonic sound with some neat orchestrations. This is an album where every song (to me) feels basically perfect. You have 'Munich' and 'Let Them Come When They Will' which are your longer prog compositions, then there's 'Asylum', 'Goodbye Post Office Tower Goodbye', and 'Survivor' which are some shorter fun rock songs. 'Reprieved' is a short, jazzy, piano-led instrumental, and 'Lisa' is a great, shorter prog song with a lot of organs. I will say the song 'Summer Weekend Of A Lifetime' is quite boring to me and sort of feels like a filler song where the band had space for one more track and just threw together a little song. I love the orchestration in this album, particularly in the two longer, prog-ier tracks. 'Munich' also has this amazing epic sounding ending with a lot of brass instruments that I personally love. Those brass instruments can also be heard on the track 'Survivor'. This album is filled to the brim with organ and guitar solos, which I enjoy but may throw some listeners off.In short, if you're a fan of symphonic orchestrations and lots of guitar and organ solos, this is the perfect album for you.Oh yeah, did you know Mikael Akerfeldt of Opeth loves this band and album? (Stated in an interview with Progrock magazine in 2004)

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Sweden has a rich history of instrumental progressive rock bands, and the current generation ofartists has some really refreshing things to offer. Stockholm's very own G�sta Berling Saga is oneof these contemporary acts - initially an underground project that slowly gained recognition, thisfour-piece band is now a familiar name in prog circles, and as of 2026 have an impressive sevenstudio albums to their name. 2018 saw the release of 'ET EX' on Sony-owned label Inside Out Music,which would be the band's fifth album. GBS play a fascinating style of instrumental progressive rockthat incorporates elements of symphonic rock, RIO, space rock, and electronica, while the quality ofthe music they create ranges from experimental to dark and expressive - overall, the mixture ofinfluences this band exhibits is quite eclectic. However, 'ET EX' deviates a little from their firstcouple of albums, as it showcases a gloomy synth-laden electronic sound, which has been noted byother reviewers as well.It is almost as if there is a retro synthwave allusion going on, as the listener encounters a vastrange of synthesizer sounds, Mellotrons, and domineering electronic hooks. These are fused reallywell with the rock instruments, by the way, as we hear tons of angular guitar riffs and hypnotic,almost Krautrock-ish rhythms. The atmosphere of this album is undoubtedly darker, but the music isso inventive and tense that one might not necessarily notice the contrasting moods. And so, thesolemn opener 'Veras Tema' leads us to the nearly 8-minute-long song 'The Shortcomings ofEfficiency', where some serpentine guitars forge an upbeat, epic-sounding prog that is quitemesmerizing, too. This is the only track containing vocals, incidentally, as sang by guest musicianMichael Berdan. 'Square 5' is another lengthy composition introducing some wandering electronicsounds, as the music spirals beautifully around the listener, while 'Over and Out' carries a darksynthwave retro feel, which is delightful in a way. 'Capercaillie...' is another peculiar trackreplete with hefty electronics, while the closing track 'Fundament', supposedly the album'scenterpiece, offers a variety of unusual ideas, blending quite naturally G�sta Berling Saga'sexperimental style with the overt 80s influence of 'ET EX'.There is a particularity to this album, meaning that it won't appeal to every single listener, butthe music is excellent all throughout and there is a lot to discover and dive into.

items.body: Review by UMUR — "The Blueprint Dives" is the fourth full-length studio album by Norwegian metal act Extol. The albumwas released through Century Media Records in February 2005. It�s the successor to "Synergy" fromAugust 2003. It would be the last release during their original run as Extol disbanding in 2007(they have since reunited). There have been a few lineup changes since "Synergy" as guitaristChrister Espevoll has been replaced by Ole Halvard Sveen and guitarist Ole B�rud has been replacedby a returning Tor Magne Glidje, who had a previous stint with Extol in the 1999-2001 periodalthough back then as the band�s bassist.Stylistically the material on "The Blueprint Dives" is in some ways a continuation of the technical/progressive metal style with Christian themed lyrics of "Synergy". The music features elements ofthrash metal and death metal just as "Synergy" did, but the harder edged metal elements havedecreased since the last album and there�s a lot more clean male singing on "The Blueprint Dives"than on the preceding album (harsh shouting vocals are still a part of the soundscape). Harmonyvocals are now also a part of the soundscape (already heard on album opener "Gloriana") and while"The Blueprint Dives" still features heavy riffs and drumming, it�s a very melodic and accessiblerelease, even touching alternative/heavy progressive rock territories once or twice. I guess this ishow it would sound if late era Death (the band) and late 1990s/early 2000s Enchant met up andcollaborated. Extol definitely have a unique sound which combines a lot of different musicalelements. The more concise songwriting approach of "Synergy" is continued on "The Blueprint Dives" which makesit a nicely accessible listening experience while still being sophisticated and challenging enoughnot to be easy listening. Extol are skilled composers and a very well playing unit too, soeverything on "The Blueprint Dives" is of a high quality. The same can be said about the soundproduction values. "The Blueprint Dives" features a powerful, clear, and detailed sound productionwhich suits the material perfectly. Upon conclusion "The Blueprint Dives" is an interesting stepforward for Extol. They may have lost a few fans because of the more melodic alternative rockapproach of some of the material (a track like "Lost In Dismay" probably won�t please that part ofthe fanbase), but praise must be given to them for the courage to keep evolving and they arguably dowhat they do with great passion and conviction. A 3.5 - 4 star (75%) rating is deserved.(Originally posted on Metal Music Archives).

items.body: Review by XixoTheRock — (In memory or Roger Keith "Syd" Barrett, 1945-2006, thank you for being my inspiration)Describing the two solo Syd Barrett records, is a difficult task, for a brief period of time between1965, to the early 1970's, Barrett shone bright like the sun in the sky, it is shocking to listen tohis latter works after listening through the whimsical fairy tale like psychedelia of "The piper atthe gates of dawn" and the first Pink Floyd singles, to the dark, gritty and minimalistic sound ofhis solo records (this particular style is way more accentuated on his last three Pink Floyd songs,only one of which was officially released on "A saucerful of secrets", the other 2 on the Earlyyears Pink Floyd box set). These two records illustrate a clear picture of what was going on in hislife during this difficult period for him, they act as autobiographical records if one is to analyzeart trying to get in the author's (this time, musicians) shoes, they're deeply personal and displayan amount of vulnerability seen in very few works, that's where the real impact of "The madcaplaughs" lies...it's the collapse and fall of a legend captured into music, forever to roam and findthose who need it in the right time.The overall aura the music has is somber, mellow, almost detached, yet fully captivating. Thecompositions are quite simple, usually a chord progression consisting on some major chordsintercalated with minor and minor 7 chords, with some chromatic elements and simple strumming on anacoustic guitar, this usually accompanied by Barrett's tired voice, that lazes softly over it alland an occasional synthesiser. The two exceptions that stand out to this rule here are the tracks"Octopus" (which, any musician will be captivated by, because of its strange progression andrhythmic structure) which has an upbeat tone with full band instrumentation and surreal, borderingdadaist lyrics (they remember me of Nicanor Parra in some ways! Although I doubt Barrett had everread Chilean poet Parra at this point I'm his life), and "No good trying", which is incrediblypsychedelic and feels like a mix between colourful yet dark spirals such as those seen in Van Gogh'spaintings and a dark, strong bitter tasting beverage, it also has full band instrumentation and thelyrics are the emotional pivot of the record, as these paint the clearest picture of what Barrettwas trying to express. Despite not being as psychedelic as his previous works, and it all being alittle more simple and amateurish, it's s collection of interesting songs, yes, they're not foreveryone and will not suit the taste of those who seek a complex, detail rich kind of music, butthose who love folk rock and want to get to know Barrett more, will love this kind of music!I really won't get too deep in the production, since it really isn't that special, it suits therecord very well and does a good job at keeping fidelity to the songs, nonetheless I'd like to addthat it was done by none other than his former bandmates and friends David Gilmour and RichardWrigth, who he wouldn't see for some years after the release of his two records, they also acted asstudio musicians (tis but a fun fact that adds even more emotional weight to the overallexperience).The picture the record paints is clear and speaks louder than any biography ever could, since it'scoming right out of our crazy diamond's soul, it serves to humanize the legend and to give acomforting (yet unsettling for those who know it's context) hug to the listener...if you're in foran emotional experience go on, but I warn you that it's not an easy listen and might not be foreveryone, but, if you like Pink Floyd, and want a refreshing record, you'll fall in love with this!Despite knowing he won't ever read this, since he's sadly passed in 2006, thank you very much,Roger, for being my inspiration and giving me moments of comfort amidst hardship, you'll be ineveryone's memories.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — It was 1977...and it truly was a whirlwind with the number of scenes happening simultaneously. New York's CBGB club was a breeding ground where bands like Television, who were killing it with Marquee Moon, Blondie, and even the early B-52s, who were as wild as aliens from outer space who had arrived from the 1950s. It was against this backdrop that Talking Heads emerged; having started as a trio in 1975, and initially championed by Lou Reed, who, like John Cale, had seen them at CBGB, the group was ready to record once Jerry Harrison joined on rhythm guitar and keyboards.Between David Byrne's vocals, distinctive right from the start, and Chris Frantz's steel pan, the band had something unique... setting them apart from their peers on the scene, even though they sounded just as raw as everyone else in a live setting. But where they truly made a difference was in their songwriting; the songs had a peculiar construction, all springing from Byrne's mind. "New Feeling" was a prime example of this experimental approach, and the quartet sounded tight and well-oiled.Within the New Wave vehicle, they incorporated rock with punk-like energy, without actually being punk, as well as soul, country, and the backing vocals found in "Tentative Decisions"; meanwhile, traces of Velvet Underground influence can be glimpsed in "Happy Day." "No Compassion" is very interesting; Tina Weymouth's bass work really stands out. There was already a distinctive sound present in Brian Eno's solo work, specifically during his collaborations with Percy Jones, though not in a fusion style, and one can even draw a line connecting it to early R.E.M. in the early 80s."The Book I Read" showcases a powerful voice, one that still had some maturing to do but was already fully present, possessing something of the vocal richness of Adrian Belew. It features a closing coda that could easily fit onto a solo album by Belew, who would later go on to work with the band. A Latin vibe takes over "First Week / Last Week... Carefree," featuring a guest saxophonist (albeit an uncredited one)."Psycho Killer" will forever be the band's classic track, with its driving, funky, provocative opening and Byrne's "psychiatric" vocal delivery; he knew exactly what he was doing, much like Roger Daltrey stuttering his way through "My Generation." The music, phrasing, and lyrics all come together to create an immortal classic and one of many generational anthems. The guitar strumming echoes the cacophonies of The Velvet Underground, the band they grew up listening to."Pulled Up" brings the debut to a close with raw, high-octane energy, a first effort that still had details to refine, yet showcased a style destined to mature beautifully over the next three albums without sacrificing energy or originality. It defied conventions and labels, embracing the freedom found in appearing normal within a world that was (and remains) increasingly anything but.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Several changes had taken place since the debut of Dave Stewart's band; there was only one track featuring vocals by Peter Blegvad, and John Greaves was on bass. There is a greater presence of wind instruments, which slow down both the fast-paced guitar passages and the keyboard sections. At times, "The Bryden 2-Step (for Amphibians) Part 1" takes on a somewhat anthemic quality (like Freeway Jam, by Jeff Beck), while at other moments it becomes more playful and slightly distorted."The Collapso" continues in a rock vein, sharing common ground with U.K.; however, Dave Stewart's highly disruptive keyboard interventions form a strong trio with the bass and drums, joined by the guitar, creating an atonal atmosphere almost reminiscent of Gentle Giant, before revisiting the same melody with a shift in pitch and rhythm. 'The Collapso' becomes an essay of multiple variations on the same melody, yet always distinct.Squarer for Maud, featuring cello and oboe, occupies another dimension entirely; yet other Stewart-led bands also updated their sound in 1978, such as Egg, with far more complex pieces by Phil Miller that take on a dramatic quality thanks to the organ backing. The oboe plays free jazz, accompanied by the rest of the band at a frenetic pace, until the piano stands alone like an island amidst Peter Blegvad's spoken-word delivery, a moment of calm before Phil Miller's return. With a string section that could belong on an Art Zoyd album.Of Queues and Cures is definitely their most rock-oriented album, yet it is well-balanced with the Canterbury essence and a style featuring wild, distorted keyboards sharing the spotlight with the guitar on "Dreams Wide Awake", a track that feels like an endless jam session, yet contains a melody full of groove and emotion at its core. On "Binoculars," John Greaves sings, his effective deep voice tracing the sinuous melodies laid out by his bandmates, while Jimmy Hastings' flute offers a most welcome, sweet gift, adding sonic variety; the display case on the album cover, with its jars full of mysteries, recalls the school library that Malcolm McDowell and his friends stormed in Lindsay Anderson's 1968 film If.... Ten years later, Dave Stewart would storm listeners' ears, using trumpets and trombones to craft a melody that snapped us out of any trivial monotony."Phl'kat'n" is another nod, somewhere between Zeuhl and Zappa, that allows "The Bryden 2-Step (for Amphibians) Part 2" to kick off with an avant-garde flair, a cutting-edge spirit that sweeps everything before it; John Greaves on bass and Dave Stewart on keyboards launch into a solid jazz-rock section before plunging into the depths, as the title suggests, and quietly fading away... because one doesn't need to make noise to go down in history.

items.body: Jabulile Majola sings “Baba Wethu” as a dove worn down by its journey, “Ngijuba elifuna indawo yokuphumula“, crossing hills and gullies through steady rain in search of somewhere to rest. When the bird’s strength gives out it calls up to heaven, the same cry each time over a marching chant, “Ulaphi sekonakala“, “where are you when things fall apart”, to the Father the isiZulu title names. The bird calling out for a Father is a boy who was left. The lyric opens on “Uthando lwangishiya ngisase mncane”, love left him while he was still a child, and he sings it from his own life: his mother vanished when he was days old, and by the age of two a pastor’s family was raising him among 26 children in rural Greytown, KwaZulu-Natal. He took the name she left him. It is all he has of her. The prayer turns before it ends. Majola reaches for a hand, “esangithunga ndawonye”, the hand that stitched him together, and asks it to lead him through the mist and across to the far side, “Ithemba eliyongiwelisa ngaphesheya”, the hope that will carry him over. He opened the song too worn to go on and ends it asking to be carried the rest of the way. He wrote “Baba Wethu” with his oldest brother, Levit Phungula. The song opens IPASI, his coming debut album, and follows his 2025 EP Isitifiketi. The live take comes from the Baxter Theatre in Rondebosch, Cape Town, where Ross Dorkin of Cape Town afropop trio Beatenberg joins Majola on bass. items.body: This is Deutsche Grammophon’s fourth album of Joe Hisaishi’s music. One recording (played by the Royal Philharmonic) is A Symphonic Celebration of selected film scores, but the others, including this latest release, focus on concert music. Metaphysica Amazon Presto Apple The album opens with Hisaishi’s Symphony No. 3 “Metaphysica”. The work was premiered by the New Japan Philharmonic in 2021 and was inspired by the music of Gustav Mahler: Hisaishi says it uses the same orchestration as Mahler’s first symphony, and it was programmed with that work at the premiere. The composer writes that the subtitle “Metaphysica” (Latin for “metaphysics”) refers to a philosophy “concerning the understanding of existence and knowledge.” The music “emphasizes logic that transcends sensation and experience,” and, in his words, “I aimed to create music composed solely of the movement of sound.” In three movements, the first (titled “existence”) is built around a rhythm “consisting of three sixteenth notes” that is heard in each movement, with “melodic movements that transform upon this foundation.” The second (“where are we going?”) grows from a single 26-measure phrase subjected to all manner of variations. The finale (“substance”) is built on a hexatonic scale which, in the composer’s words, is “placed on both the time and spatial axis.” I am hesitant to critique a composer’s style, as listeners’ tastes differ and my reaction may not be shared by others. So let me state straight away that Hisaishi is a minimalist, a school of composition I have struggled to understand and appreciate for most of my life. His orchestration is expert and was the most enjoyable aspect of my listening. One can find online descriptions of his memorable melodies, but I did not find that to be the case here. Nor does the symphony use expected Classical-Romantic structures: in the outer movements I listened for elements of sonata form, in which multiple themes are presented, developed, and recapitulated. Instead, Hisaishi builds his music by presenting a melodic motive and subjecting it to coloristic variation. That orchestration held my interest for a long stretch; Hisaishi’s music is atmospheric and cinematic. But the three-note rhythm meant to bind the three movements together was not evident to me, even after repeated listening, nor was the melodic writing memorable. The ostinatos and continuing variations felt overused, and by the third movement I struggled to stay focused on the music. Excepting continuous variation, I am not sure how Hisaishi’s music connects to Mahler’s symphonic world, though his notes on the symphony suggest that was his intent. Not a revelatory discovery for me, though others may react differently. Joe Hisaishi. Photo © Nick Rutter. The Harp Concerto was a joint commission by the Los Angeles Philharmonic, the Bordeaux National Opera, the Philharmonie de Paris, and the Singapore Symphony Orchestra, written for Emmanuel Ceysson, the Los Angeles Philharmonic’s principal harpist. Ceysson collaborated with the composer, both in Los Angeles and Japan, during its composition. Deutsche Grammophon’s notes state that the work “reimagines the expressive possibilities of the harp,” replacing “conventional notions of delicacy with driving rhythms, bold gestures, and striking emotional intensity.” The concerto proved a more engaging listening experience. I sensed less reliance on ostinato writing — or perhaps the more substantial melodic writing and Western harmonic progressions made it seem so. The writing is more memorable; even after the first listening, parts of the work remained in my head. And the music does succeed in reimagining the instrument’s expressive possibilities, especially in the outer movements, which feature dazzling playing from Ceysson. The highlight for me, though, was the poignant second movement, which ends with a substantial coda demonstrating both the technique and musicianship of the soloist. Disappointingly, the digital release does not include any liner notes. The Royal Philharmonic play splendidly, though they sound more engaged by the concerto than the symphony. The recording is spacious and clear. One assumes that with the composer conducting, the music goes exactly as he intends. items.body: Une Vraie Gothique – literally translated as A True Goth – is a French duo that came into existence in Paris in 2023, founded by Ulrika and Ferdinand Legendre. This year, Manic Depression Records released their debut album, “R.D.V. Au Cimetière”, an eclectic take on dark Electronic music where EBM, Dark-Wave and Techno collide. Their identity is every bit as important as their music: corpse paint, dark humor, French and German lyrics, and a generous wink towards the codes and clichés of Goth culture all come together to create a universe that is at once serious, absurd and irresistibly danceable. The album’s nine tracks take the listener on a journey into a world where darkness and absurdity go hand in hand. A defining element of the record is the interplay between the two voices: Ulrika sings in German, while Ferdinand delivers his vocals in French, making many of the tracks feel like a dark and intriguing dialogue. For me personally, this debut is an absolute revelation. A band whose name may initially sound like the ultimate Goth cliché – although I see it much more as a hilarious reference to the scene that clearly inspires them – manages to turn those very clichés on their head. The real strength and originality of Une Vraie Gothique lie in their compositions. They crack open the codes of different genres and reshape them into something distinctly their own, creating what feels much more like an ode to underground Electronic music than a parody of it. “R.D.V. Au Cimetière” is one of those albums I was instantly sold on. So, it is high time to get to know Ulrika and Ferdinand from Une Vraie Gothique a little better and discover what exactly lies behind the corpse paint, the French and German incantations, and that irresistible urge to meet somewhere in the cemetery… (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) MD176 – UNE VRAIE GOTHIQUE "R.D.V. au Cimetière" by Une Vraie Gothique Une Vraie Gothique interview Q: Could you tell us how you first met and how that eventually led to the creation of Une Vraie Gothique? Were there any particular artists or albums that served as important points of reference in shaping your sound? Ferdinand: We met at a mutual friend’s house, and Ulrika had asked me to help her compose an Electro-Disco track on the theme of the tiger for a performance she was doing at a Parisian cabinet of curiosities. Our conversations about music led us to realize our shared love of Goth music. So we decided to launch this project, starting with the title track, “Une Vraie Gothique.” We don’t really have any major points of reference, but I’d say we’re influenced by a huge number of different projects. For my part, Suicide Commando and Hocico immediately come to mind, for example. Ulrika: When that tiger project was finished, we had a sleepover where we were supposed to start working on a Euro-Dance track (one of our guilty pleasures). But instead, we watched “Hellraiser”, sampled ‘Demons to Some, Angels to Others’, (which you can hear at the beginning of our track “Une Vraie Gothique” ) and the process of becoming a true Goth was set in motion! I wish I could tell you another story and say that we probably connected in immaterial realms long before we met four years ago, but that’s still a topic under investigation. Q: I imagine the band’s name is meant to be taken with a touch of humor, but I’m still curious about the story behind it. Why did you choose Une Vraie Gothique, and if it does refer to Gothic culture, what does that scene and its music represent to you personally? Ulrika: We get asked a lot about this. Do I relate to the Goth scene and culture? Definitely. Come on, I was reading all classical Goth books, from Ann Radcliffe to Baudelaire, watching my classmates out of the corner of my eye in high school, while taking refuge in the school cloister to take black-and-white photos in long dresses. Do I see myself as a ‘genuine gothic’? Of course no. No one could… let’s then joke about it? In fact, I don’t think seriousness and humor are incompatible, except in Kundera’s “The Joke”, which deals with a totalitarian system. For me, the Goth scene is that undeniable feeling of being at home. I go down into a basement, drawn by the light and the sounds, by the promise of an intensity that’s both painful and joyful. Bodies dancing, minor scales. It’s already a contradiction in itself! The Goth scene is about celebrating life, with one foot in another world (the world of the dead, the world of shadows?). There’s a kind of haunting ritual, wrapped in a contemporary aesthetic. I wanna be a part of it, as a priestess. Ferdinand: Goth music represents my musical ‘family’. I discovered it through a sampler from Elegy magazine around 2003, and even though I developed my musical taste by listening to a wide variety of genres, it was Goth music that most gave me that sense of ‘belonging’ to a musical family. It was also at these parties that I danced the most and watched others dance. Among Goths, as in any social group, there are certain attitudes and recurring elements that you can have fun with while still respecting them. My friends and I have always had a great sense of self-deprecating humor, and we loved to laugh at ourselves. At first, we couldn’t quite come to terms with the fact that we were goths, even though we were clearly identified as such by everyone outside the movement who interacted with us. I think “Une Vraie Gothique” tells this story—the playful questioning of a genre’s identity that sometimes tells its followers, ‘If you want to be different, be like us’. In this project, we’re trying to strike the right balance: the band is perfectly accessible at face value (especially because of Ulrika’s character, who talks almost exclusively about personal things), but you can also have fun reading between the lines to uncover humorous elements. Q: Strictly speaking, your music doesn’t sound traditionally Gothic. Instead, it blends elements of EBM, Electro-Wave and even Techno, while it’s mainly the atmosphere and the song titles that evoke a Gothic aesthetic. How would you describe your musical identity, and how do you see the relationship between your Electronic sound and the themes explored in your lyrics? Ferdinand: Ulrika and I both listen to a huge variety of very different music. I’ve listened to a lot of Techno, actually, and quite a bit of Rap, which comes through in some of the tracks and in the way I use my voice at times. I think you’re right: the music itself isn’t necessarily ‘Goth’ in the traditional sense. It’s more of a reflection of a movement that has evolved and influenced many different musical styles. I feel like we’re living in an amazing era for music. Things are much less compartmentalized than before. There are Pop bands with a Goth aesthetic; Techno has become much darker; and many people in Hip-Hop don’t hesitate to rock leather and latex looks. We use elements that come from all over the place and that serve the purpose of the tracks: metal clangs, animal sounds, and a variety of synths and VSTs. We want our tracks to be hard-hitting and dark; we compose from the heart, and we’re our own biggest fans. Even if we wanted to make an entire album consisting solely of dark Electro tracks, I’m not sure we could pull it off. We’re diverse by nature. Ulrika: I like the opportunity to create my own music and follow my own, personal and unique vision. As I said in the previous question, I am definitely truly and completely related to the Goth/dark/alternative scene. BUT I want to be true to myself also, and I have to recognize different parts I am made of. To me, our musical identity is soft & sexy. The scent of Père Lachaise Cemetery on a windy day. Why? We often have a sultry bass line and pleasant, mellow mid-range frequencies. And I use my voice in a percussive, unsettling, incantatory way (the graves), whilst also allowing myself to incorporate more lyrical and mystical elements (the great wind). My influences are related to Germany: Deine Lakaien, Welle:Erdball, Helium Vola, Sopor Aeternus, Lacrimas Profundere, Agonoize, Feindflug, Nina Hagen, Bohren & Der Club Of Gore… as far as possible, I preferred to listen to German lyrics and, as I was in Metz in my childhood (East of France), it made more sense to look across the border. As for the Electronic aspect, I just want to say that I love powerful basslines and energetic kicks, paired with melodies you can really let loose to. In our lyrics, we’re always talking about connection and energy. ‘Electronics’ comes from ‘electron’. It’s what carries electricity. I feel like I’m right at the heart of my material theme! Q: How did the two of you collaborate on “R.D.V. Au Cimetière”? What roles does each of you take on within the creative process, and what were the biggest challenges you encountered during the writing, recording and production of the album? Ulrika: Thanks for this question. It’s great to talk about the creative process! For me, the biggest challenge is finding our signature style, our identity, our voice. We’re walking a tightrope between our influences and our own inner worlds. I’ve made huge progress writing this album by allowing myself to simplify and pare down musical phrases to give them more impact. I’d like to do that even more. We also try to focus on using variations rather than introducing new elements when we want the song to evolve. One of our favorite questions now is, ‘What if we did a bass variation?’. Right after ‘What filter should we put on the keyboard?’ Ferdinand: We’re both involved in every stage of the songwriting process. We both write and compose equally. Sometimes one of us needs to spend a few hours working on the song alone, and then we come back to it together, but overall we work as a team. Usually, I start by suggesting a rhythm and bassline, and Ulrika adds variations to it, then fairly quickly brings in vocal elements and a narrative direction. Sometimes we work together, and sometimes we take turns, but we always end up with a song to which we’ve both contributed equally. The biggest challenge was undoubtedly not going off in all directions. There were times when we took the humor too far, for example, and the song became way too parodic, so we had to completely backtrack. As mentioned earlier, our main challenge is finding the right balance between paying homage to that scene and allowing for different levels of interpretation.Q: You are based in Paris, which seems to have become an increasingly vibrant hub for both the Electronic and Gothic underground scenes. What is it like to be part of that environment? Does a city like Paris influence artists in a way comparable to cities such as Berlin, or does it have its own unique creative identity? Ferdinand: Paris is lucky to have so many ‘underground’ venues and an endless cultural heritage. The walls have a history, and there are so many people that you always end up meeting others who are interested in what you’re offering and who understand your vision. We also have a vibrant cultural scene in the suburbs—I’m thinking of cities like Montreuil, for example, which have always been very open to alternative ideas. I don’t know if our city influences us the way Berlin might, but it certainly offers us plenty of opportunities to connect with others. Ulrika : I find inspiration in old places. I love cemeteries, and coming across churches, works of art, and objects from the 12th century is definitely a source of enchantment. I studied at the school of the Louvre, which had a profound impact on me. That’s why I chose to live in Paris. Besides, it’s the only city I know where I can go to a medieval music concert of Hildegard von Bingen or Perrotin on Monday, a Black-Metal show on Tuesday, a math lecture on Wednesday, an Electro-Goth show on Thursday, and a batcave show on Friday. We’re incredibly lucky to be surrounded by this beautiful heritage, and I want to honor and share it. I feel enriched by this multicultural history of dark music from today and yesterday, sometimes looking back several centuries ! Q: Have you already started working on new Une Vraie Gothique material or other projects? Looking back at “R.D.V. Au Cimetière”, how critical are you of the album today? Are there aspects you’re particularly proud of, and are there things you would approach differently next time? Ulrika: We are currently working on a documentary that we filmed in February 2026 in California at the Mars College Festival. We had the immense pleasure of being invited by Vanessa Rosa and Gene Kogan to the desert to collaborate with the artists/developers and create a song about Euler’s Basel formula, in which we seek to convey the emotional impact of a theoretical argument. That’s my ultimate quest! We’re finishing up the composition of the song and wrapping up the editing! Is math Gothic? It’s full of formulas, after all. As for the album, this is my first release with this kind of project. There are inevitably things we’d like to take further, but I’m extremely proud of the work we’ve done, and I enjoy listening to the tracks without feeling like they’re mine. That’s a good sign! Moving forward, I’d like to simplify things even more, making them even more effective and precise. Asking myself, ‘What can we take away?’ rather than ‘What can we add?’ ‘Less is more’ (Mies van der Rohe) is a powerfull statement. Ferdinand: I’m very proud of this debut album; it really captures our work and the first narrative arc of Une Vraie Gothique. That said, I can’t wait to release new material, and we’re already working on the next album. In fact, we’re playing several songs live that aren’t on “R.D.V. Au Cimetière” but will be on the next one, such as “France Gothique” or the more recent “Anathème.” I think we’ve both grown in many ways; I don’t think there’s any aspect we’ll need to approach fundamentally differently next time. We’re going to keep putting out great songs and try to get our music out there at festivals and abroad. We’re also very happy with our first music video, “Nuée Ardente,” directed by Anaïs Novembre, which brings a welcome new visual dimension to the project.

items.body: De/Vision released their synth-pop album “Fairyland?” on 9 August 1996 through Strange Ways Records. The album turns 30 this year. It became the first De/Vision album to enter the German album charts, where it reached number 87 later that month. ‘Fairyland?’, De/Vision’s first chart entry The band recorded the album at The Factory in Belgium in April and May 1996. De/Vision produced and mixed the record together with José Alvarez-Brill, and Tom Meyer mastered it at Master & Servant in Hamburg. Strange Ways Records issued “Fairyland?” on CD, alongside a limited digipak edition of 7,777 copies that came with a 12-page booklet and a band poster. The twelve tracks are “I Regret,” “Dawn,” “Sweet Life,” “Like the Sun,” “Harvester,” “Today’s Life,” “Scars,” “Keep Your Dreams Alive,” “Wages of Sin,” “Bleed Me White,” “Take Me to the Time…” and “Daydreamin’.” The singles “I Regret” and “Sweet Life” accompanied the album in 1996. The album entered the German album charts on 26 August 1996 and peaked at number 87, the band’s first chart placement. Asked in a Q&A on their Apple Music artist page about the most memorable moments of their career, the band pointed straight to this record: “Our first chart success with ‘Fairyland?’ in 1996!” The live album “Fairylive!” followed in 1997. The original 1996 recordings are currently not available on the major streaming services; the album circulates on CD through the secondhand market. About De/Vision De/Vision formed in July 1988 in Bensheim, near Darmstadt, Germany, with Steffen Keth on vocals and Thomas Adam, Markus Ganssert and Stefan Blender on synthesizers. Blender left in 1991. The band self-released the single “Your Hands on My Skin” in 1990 and issued “Boy on the Street” in 1992 through Synthetic Product Records, before the 1993 maxi single “Try to Forget” brought them to Strange Ways Records. The debut album “World Without End” followed in 1994, produced by Axel Henninger, who had previously worked with Camouflage. “Unversed in Love” and “Antiquity” both appeared in 1995, and “Fairyland?” arrived in August 1996 as the band’s first chart album. “Monosex” followed in 1998 through WEA. Markus Ganssert left in 2000, and Keth and Adam have continued as a duo since, now based in Berlin. They founded their own label Popgefahr Records in 2009 and released later albums including “Popgefahr” (2010), “Rockets and Swords” (2012), “13” (2016) and “Citybeats” (2018). Keth also appears in Devision Redux, which went on tour in 2025 with Daniel Myer of Haujobb, while De/Vision themselves joined a 2025 tour with Lakeside X and Empathy Test. The 30th anniversary of “Fairyland?” points back to the album that opened that chart history.

items.body: Carpenter Brut and HEALTH will reunite this autumn for “Conflict: Europe 2026”, the European continuation of their co-headlining partnership following the North American “Conflict: Leather Tour” earlier this year. The European run begins in Utrecht on November 3 and moves through the UK, Germany, Poland, Hungary and Italy, with VOWWS joining as special guests on the joint dates. The pairing works precisely because the two headliners arrive at heaviness from different directions. Carpenter Brut builds it through darksynth, metal dynamics, huge synthesizer hooks and cinematic excess, while HEALTH combine industrial electronics, distorted guitars, noise and vulnerable melodic songwriting. On the same bill, these approaches should create a particularly physical evening without simply repeating the same musical language twice. For Polish audiences, the tour brings two consecutive shows: November 16, 2026 – Kraków, Klub Studio – Carpenter Brut + HEALTH + VOWWS November 17, 2026 – Wrocław, Centrum Koncertowe A2 – Carpenter Brut + HEALTH + VOWWS The Polish concerts are promoted by Knock Out Productions. The European dates come after Carpenter Brut and HEALTH spent spring 2026 touring North America together, making this less of a one-off package and more of an ongoing collaboration between two acts whose audiences increasingly overlap across industrial, dark electronic, alternative and heavier scenes. ‘Conflict: Europe 2026’ tour dates Carpenter Brut, HEALTH and VOWWS play the following joint dates: November 3 – Utrecht, Netherlands – TivoliVredenburg November 4 – Bristol, UK – O2 Academy Bristol November 5 – Glasgow, UK – SWG3 Galvanizers November 6 – Wolverhampton, UK – Wulfrun Hall November 11 – Hamburg, Germany – Große Freiheit 36 November 13 – Leipzig, Germany – Täubchenthal November 16 – Kraków, Poland – Klub Studio November 17 – Wrocław, Poland – Centrum Koncertowe A2 November 19 – Budapest, Hungary – Barba Negra November 20 – Milan, Italy – Alcatraz About HEALTH HEALTH is an American industrial rock band formed in Los Angeles in 2005 by vocalist and guitarist Jake Duzsik and bassist John Famiglietti, who met while Duzsik was working at a Guitar Center store. Guitarist Jupiter Keyes and drummer BJ Miller joined soon after, giving the band its early lineup; Keyes left in 2015, and the group has continued as the trio of Duzsik, Famiglietti and Miller. HEALTH drew early attention with a remix of Crystal Castles’ “Crimewave” before releasing its self-titled debut album in 2007, followed by “Get Color” in 2009 and “Death Magic” via Loma Vista Recordings in 2015. “Vol. 4 :: Slaves of Fear” followed in 2019, and the band released the collaborative “Disco4” project across two volumes in 2020 and 2022. HEALTH issued “Rat Wars” in 2023, and its sixth studio album, “Conflict DLC”, followed via Loma Vista Recordings on December 11, 2025, preceded by the singles “Ordinary Loss”, “Vibe Cop”, “Thought Leader”, “You Died”, “Shred Envy” and “Antidote”. Los Angeles-based HEALTH have spent years developing a sound in which industrial electronics, noise, metal and pop melody are allowed to coexist without softening one another. One of the band’s most distinctive qualities remains the contrast between the enormous physical weight of the production and Duzsik’s comparatively restrained, vulnerable vocal delivery, which gives the music an emotional character very different from straightforward industrial aggression. The current touring cycle follows “Conflict DLC”, continuing the darker and heavier direction explored on “Rat Wars”. Live, that combination of mechanical rhythm, distortion and unexpectedly intimate vocals gives HEALTH a particularly strong physical and emotional presence, one that carries directly into the “Conflict: Europe 2026” dates. About Carpenter Brut Carpenter Brut is the project of French producer Franck Hueso, born in 1977 in Poitiers, who has cultivated anonymity as a deliberate artistic choice since starting the project in 2012 to mix horror-film scoring, metal, rock and electronic music. He first released three EPs, “EP I” (2012), “EP II” (2013) and “EP III” (2015), later compiled as the debut album “Trilogy” (2015). “Leather Teeth” followed in 2018, drawing on 1980s metal and glam rock and opening the fictional story of anti-hero Bret Halford. Hueso then scored the animated feature “Blood Machines” in 2020 before continuing the narrative with “Leather Terror” in 2022. He closed the trilogy with Leather Temple, released on February 27, 2026, which continues Bret Halford’s story into a cryogenic, cyberpunk-inflected future and closes out the “Leather” arc that began with “Leather Teeth”. Carpenter Brut approaches electronic heaviness from another angle than HEALTH. His music draws from synthwave, metal, horror cinema and 1980s pop culture, but over the years the project has moved far beyond simple retro aesthetics, developing into something much more aggressive, theatrical and designed for large live spaces. “Leather Temple” continues Carpenter Brut’s mixture of cinematic electronics, darksynth and metal while expanding the fictional world that has accompanied this chapter of the project, material that now anchors the “Conflict: Europe 2026” set. With VOWWS opening and two headliners whose methods of creating tension are so different, “Conflict: Europe 2026” looks like one of the more interesting dark electronic touring packages of the autumn, including the two Polish dates in Kraków and Wrocław.

items.body: 6YPAH is a Slovenian/Italian duo releasing their debut album here. It appears to be a conceptual work inspired by the early years of the Soviet space program and the space race with the USA. The duo crafted this six-track album primarily using analog equipment. The opening track immediately transports us to a bygone musical era, perfectly matching the album’s concept. Clear Krautrock influences are evident, with the psychedelic guitar taking center stage. Gradually, a balance develops between guitar and electronics, with the warm analog textures adding further depth. The music consistently evokes a sense of nostalgia, at times leaning toward an ’80s aesthetic and even incorporating touches of Wave-Pop. Vocals are present throughout, although they serve more as an additional layer than as the main focus of the compositions. This strikes me as the kind of album that truly benefits from a visual component, allowing its concept to unfold to its fullest. It is a highly commendable debut that will especially appeal to a discerning audience. (Rating:6½). Listen to “Vedno S Tabo”: Vedno S Tabo by 6YPAH About 6YPAH 6YPAH is a Slovenian duo formed in Nova Gorica in 2009 by singer and keyboardist Jani Toplak and guitarist and bassist Giorgio Multineddu. The project calls itself “transboundary,” pairing Slovenian songwriting with a base that stretches across the nearby Italian border into Gorizia. 6YPAH mixes synthwave with krautrock and 1970s and 1980s German electronic influences, and sings in Slovene. The duo self-released its first recording, “Electronic Visions Across The Border” (CDr, catalog RSSCD02), in 2023. 6YPAH then signed to Final Muzik for “Prozorno Mesto,” a concept album inspired by the Soviet Buran space program and the space race with the United States. Bandcamp lists the release date as 7 April 2026, while Discogs dates the release to 2025. The album was recorded and mixed at Resounding Sounds Studio in Gorizia, Italy, and mastered by Gregor Zemljic in Ljubljana, Slovenia. Guitarist Matteo Birsa performs a guest solo on “Vedno S Tabo.” The album’s limited CD edition is capped at 200 copies, tying this release to the duo’s ongoing work built around analog synthesizers and Cold War-era imagery.
